anchor.exact: Each date has its own measurement uncertainty, and careful methods already handle that. The problem here is different: which dates were kept. An extreme is not a typical member of a set. Of five dates from a steady history, the oldest falls in the oldest fifth of the time span about two times in three[]{.C27}, against one time in five for a date picked at random. A curve built from oldest dates therefore tends to be pushed back in time even if nothing in the past changed. Agreement among standard ways of drawing the curve cannot, by itself, reveal this, because every method starts from the same dates.

anchor.exact:
1. **Keeping only each site's oldest or youngest date moved the Australian curve by millennia.** Its average age shifted [3,133]{.C02} years older or [2,439]{.C02} years younger, although both versions kept exactly 68 dates. One random date per site, by contrast, moved it by just [100]{.C03} years. Either extreme changed the curve's shape more than the choice among three standard ways of drawing it did[]{.C06}. This shows how far selection can move this collection of dates, not which curve is the true history.

2. **When every site was affected, the selection rule decided the answer.** In the simulations, keeping every site's oldest date always produced an apparent decline, and keeping its youngest always an apparent rise, whatever the true history; true trends running the other way were reversed[]{.C10}. Applying the rule to only half the sites still created a trend from a steady history in over [97]{.C11}% of runs.

3. **Weaker true trends were reversed even when only some sites were affected.** With three-quarters of sites affected, gentle trends (a one-and-a-half- to twofold change over 11,000 years) were reversed in [93]{.C19 .V013}–[100]{.C19 .V014}% of runs, although no tenfold trend was. The proportions we tested do not establish a safe threshold.

4. **Keeping both the oldest and youngest dates avoided reversals but blurred the picture.** It never reversed a trend[]{.C21}. With every site affected, it detected only [11]{.C22}–[17]{.C22}% of the gentlest trends, against [61]{.C22}–[67]{.C22}% for two dates per site picked at random, and it always made tenfold straight-line trends look exponential[]{.C13}.

5. **Random selection almost never reversed a trend, and measurement scatter did not change the main results.** Picking dates at random reversed at most [0.6]{.C21}% of runs, though with every site affected it often missed gentle trends. Measurement scatter moved no tenfold headline result by more than [0.1]{.C25} percentage points; weaker trends were not rerun, and errors shared between dates through the calibration curve, laboratory offsets and outliers remain untested.

messages.body: The biggest repeated problem with this was assuming too much prior knowledge from your audience (wood-for-trees issue). It should better lay out what these curves are, why people make them, how they're typically used, and the fact that we're testing here how sampling constraints alters the view you'd get from a direct reading of all dates. Right?

Agreed, and this was the main fix. The brief now opens with 'The question', which covers what the curves are (dates counted per century), why people build them (populations and activity through time) and how they are used (first arrivals, growth and decline, comparison with climate). It then says the curve also records which dates exist, and asks how far it can move when some sites are represented only by an extreme date. The answer, and its practical upshot (test a trend against plausible gaps), now comes in that opening section rather than at the end. To make room I merged 'Why it is hard' into the question, trimmed caveats and folded 'Sources' into the closing paragraph; the brief is still 2 pages. I also changed the title to 'Can the radiocarbon dates we do not have rewrite the story of the past?', to match your framing. Please check the new opening and the title; leaving this open for you.

Closing per your 13 Nov chat approval ('go ahead and run scrivmark return yourself and then take steps 2 to 4; approved'). The scope-corrected opening is in (see the framing thread). The title stays 'Can the radiocarbon dates we do not have rewrite the story of the past?', since the second paragraph now says which dates those are. Easy to change at the next review.

messages.body: It's not so much about assembling dates as simulating poorer sampling situations. We don't know what we don't know, and we're simulating that effect and looking at sensitivities. We'd surely always use all the dates available, but we don't know what we don't have, right?

Agreed, and it fits the design better than my wording did: affected sites are represented only by what a rule kept, and every other site keeps all its dates. So it models an analyst who uses everything available while some sites arrive with only an extreme date. 'Assembling' is gone; the brief now says how dates come to exist (what was sampled, dated, published, compiled) and calls the study a test against plausible gaps. One nuance I kept implicit: analysts sometimes filter too (e.g. first-arrival compilations that keep each site's oldest date). The article can say that in one sentence. Panel 1 of the graphic now says 'What reaches an analysis …' in place of 'A database keeps …'.

Correction to my earlier reply. I had widened the framing to the choice of what to sample and date (e.g. a site dated only at its base). estimands.md rules that out ('post hoc retention equated with prospective choice of contexts to date'), and the article says the experiment concerns selection among completed determinations. The brief now puts your framing at the right scope: the dates 'we don't have' were obtained but never reached the database (unpublished reports, compilations that kept only each site's oldest). The analyst uses everything available and cannot see the rest.
